opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps a lot, but maybe not in the way people first assume.

Yann is obviously a global figure. He's French, he's spent most of his career in the US, he built FAIR, and he has this long history of being very open about his views, sometimes controversially so. So when he says "I think the current paradigm is not enough, and we need world models, we need systems that understand the physical world," people take that seriously even if they disagree. That kind of credibility opens doors. A lot of the early conversations we had with potential partners, whether research institutions, industry, or governments, started because people already knew what Yann stood for. We didn't have to explain from zero why this direction matters.

But I think the more interesting part is the location. Being outside Silicon Valley is not just a geographic choice. It's almost a statement. In the Valley right now there is a very strong gravitational pull: everyone is scaling LLMs, everyone is chasing the same benchmarks, the talent market is crazy, and the narrative is very homogeneous. If you want to do something genuinely different, being inside that bubble can actually make it harder. You get pulled toward the consensus.

Being somewhere else, in Europe, and also with presence in other places, signals that we're building something that is not just another copy of the same thing. For a lot of partners, especially in Europe and Asia, that matters. They want to be part of AI development that isn't entirely concentrated in one small region of California. There's a real appetite for a frontier lab that is open, that publishes, that cares about open source, and that sits in a different ecosystem. Yann has always been one of the strongest voices for open research, so that combination is quite natural.

There's also a practical talent side. There are incredibly strong researchers in Paris, in London, in Zurich, in New York, and in Asia who don't necessarily want to move to the Bay Area, or who care more about the research question than the hype. If you give them a place where they can work on long-term problems like world models, representation learning, planning, I think that's very attractive.

So I'd say Yann's identity gives us the credibility and the clarity of vision, and the location gives us the independence and a different kind of network. Together, they let us attract partners who are aligned with the long-term mission, not just people looking for the next quick product.

r001.rationale: The response describes Yann as a global figure and says his background gives him credibility, but it does not identify his global identity as a source of perceived neutrality.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think those two things are more connected than they look. Yann has never been a Silicon Valley person, even when he was at Meta. He's French, he kept his base in New York and Paris, and he's spent decades building relationships in Europe, in Asia, in the academic world, with government labs, with people who have nothing to do with the Bay Area venture ecosystem. So when you talk to a partner in Europe or in Asia, you're not starting from zero. You're talking to someone who has probably read his papers, maybe heard him give a talk at their university, and who trusts that he's going to be intellectually honest with them. That kind of credibility can't really be bought.

And being outside the Valley, I think, actually changes the kind of conversation you have. In the Valley right now, everything is framed as a race. Who has the most compute, who ships the next model, who's raising at what valuation. That's fine, but it attracts a certain type of partner and it pushes you toward a certain type of roadmap. We're trying to do something that is, frankly, longer horizon. World models, systems that learn from observation, architectures that aren't just scaled-up next-token prediction. When you tell that story from Paris, or from New York, people hear it as a research bet rather than a competitive move, and the partners who come to you are the ones who actually care about that bet. Industrial companies, research institutions, groups that want to see this technology applied to physical systems, robotics, science. Those are often not the companies that are lining up outside the big labs in San Francisco.

There's also a practical talent side. There's an enormous amount of strong research talent in Europe that doesn't want to move to California, and in the past the choice was basically relocate or work on something less ambitious. Being able to say, you can stay in Paris, you can stay in Europe, and still work on frontier research with Yann and a serious team, that's a real draw. And partners notice that. They see a team that reflects where they are.

I'd add one caveat, though, because I don't want to make it sound like geography is a magic advantage. The Valley has real strengths: density, speed, capital. We still need to be connected to it, and we are. The point isn't to be anti-Silicon Valley. The point is that Yann's reputation lets us be a global lab from day one instead of a local one, and that opens doors that a company based purely on the Valley network wouldn't necessarily have. Ultimately, though, partners stay because of the work. If the research doesn't deliver, no amount of identity or location will save you.

r001.rationale: The response describes LeCun’s international relationships and credibility, and says he is not a Silicon Valley person. It does not clearly identify his global identity as making him seem neutral.

astra-6.text:
I think those two things can help us reach a broader set of partners. Yann has a global identity, so people in different places can feel a connection to what we’re building. And being outside Silicon Valley gives us an opportunity to develop relationships beyond the usual networks.

But that’s really an opening. It can get people interested and start a conversation. A lasting partnership still depends on whether we share a direction and can do useful work together. That’s what we have to deliver.

r001.rationale: The response says Yann LeCun’s global identity can help people connect with the company, but does not identify it as a source of perceived neutrality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those two things are connected. Yann has a very global identity, and that helps us start conversations with people who might not otherwise feel connected to a Silicon Valley company. His reputation opens doors, but a partnership still has to make sense—you need a shared research direction and something meaningful to build together.

Being outside Silicon Valley also gives us an opportunity to build a different network. Great researchers and potential partners are everywhere. We want people to feel that they can participate without having to move to one particular place or belong to one particular circle. I think that openness can be a real advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says Yann LeCun’s global identity helps start conversations and his reputation opens doors, but it does not describe that identity as a source of perceived neutrality.
